title: The beam in your eye
hookLine: first cast out the beam out of thine own eye (Matthew 7:3–5)
tomorrow: what does a house on rock sound like in a storm?

lines: A KING WHO MISSED HIS OWN.
cards: Scroll any comment section long enough and someone types "judge not" in the middle of judging somebody. Matthew 7 opens with it: "Judge not, that ye be not judged." So, yesterday's question: can you judge anyone at all?
Christians read it two ways, and both have a case. But first, a king who judged a stranger's crime in a heartbeat, and missed his own.

teach.b: In Second Samuel, King David has taken another man's wife and covered it up with that man's death. The prophet Nathan comes with a story.

A rich man with huge flocks has a guest to feed, so he takes a poor man's one little ewe lamb, a lamb the poor man raised like a daughter. David is furious: "the man that hath done this thing shall surely die."
And Nathan says, "Thou art the man." David saw the speck in a stranger and missed the beam in himself.
Jesus's picture: "why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?"
A speck of sawdust in your brother's eye, a roof timber in yours. Now the two readings.
One says judge not means just that: leave condemning to God, because "with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again."
Its best case: Jesus opens with the plain command, and the beam story shows how blind a judge can be.
The other reading points to the end of the passage: "first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye."
Its best case: Jesus expects you to help with the mote, and later in the chapter says "by their fruits ye shall know them." Both agree on the order.

how: Christians differ on how to read 'judge not' (Matthew 7:1–5): some stress leaving judgment to God, others stress self-examination first and then honest, gentle correction. In Catholic practice, an examination of conscience comes before confession.

games.q: what does “the beam in your eye” mean?
o: the bigger fault you miss in yourself while correcting others
a splinter of wood from the cross of Jesus
a sharp look of anger aimed at someone you dislike

games.q: the speck and the timber: tap the pairs.
p: a speck in your brother's eye

s: Jesus says never help anyone with their faults
after the beam: then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote.
Nathan got King David to judge himself with a story
David condemned the rich man; Nathan said, thou art the man.
in the saying, the mote and the beam are the same size
a speck in your brother's eye, a timber in your own.

games.q: your friend says 'judge not' means no one may ever call anything wrong. give the best case for the other Christian reading, as its own readers would.
o: the passage ends with seeing clearly to help remove the mote, so honest correction comes after self-examination.
the other reading says Christians may judge outsiders freely but never one another.
the other reading says 'judge not' was meant only for Jesus's first followers.
games.why: one reading leans on 7:1–2, the other on 7:5 and 'by their fruits ye shall know them'. both put the beam first.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one person whose fault you see clearly. Then, gently, turn it around: is there a smaller or bigger version of the same thing in you? Sit with what you find, without a verdict either way.

wordCard.voice: The beam in your eye: the fault you miss in yourself while you're squinting at the speck in someone else's.

orig.note: Greek, Matthew 7:3: a beam, a roof timber; the mote is karphos, a speck or splinter.

carryVoice: For the road: my own beam, before anyone else's mote. Nathan's four words still work.
